transcript.text: Bosch WTN85201GB condenser dryer not drying properly anymore, clothes still damp after 2 hrs. any ideas

Damp clothes after 2 hours on a condenser dryer like the WTN85201GB is usually caused by an airflow problem rather than a broken part. Here's what to check, starting with the easiest and most likely.

## 1. Clean the fluff filters (both of them)
• The filter is in the door opening. It's actually two parts: pull it out and open it up, then clean the inner and outer mesh.
• If it looks clean but feels "waxy" (from fabric softener residue), wash it under warm water with a soft brush and let it dry fully. A clogged mesh can look fine but block airflow.
• Check the slot the filter sits in for fluff build-up too.

## 2. Clean the condenser unit (the most common cause)
• It's behind the flap at the bottom front (kick plate). Unlock the levers and slide the condenser out.
• Rinse it with a shower head or hose from all sides until water runs through clearly. Don't use anything sharp, as the fins bend easily.
• Clean the seals and the cavity it sits in, then refit it and lock the levers properly. An incorrectly seated condenser leaks air and dries badly.
• Bosch recommends doing this roughly every 20 cycles or so. Many people never do it, and it gets matted with fluff.

## 3. Empty the water container
• Make sure it's emptied every load. If it's full, the dryer will stop or underperform. If your dryer is plumbed to a drain, check that the hose isn't kinked.

## 4. Clean the moisture sensors
• Inside the drum, near the filter, there are two metal strips. These tell the dryer when clothes are "dry."
• Softener and limescale coat them, causing the machine to stop early or misjudge dryness.
• Wipe them with a cloth and a little vinegar, or use the rough side of a sponge (non-metallic).

## 5. Check how you're using it
• Load size: Overloading means poor tumbling and airflow. Mixed heavy and light items dry unevenly.
• Spin speed: Clothes should come out of the washer spun at 1200–1400 rpm if the fabric allows. Wetter clothes take much longer.
• Programme: "Iron dry" leaves clothes slightly damp by design. Use "Cupboard dry" or "Extra dry," or a timed programme to test.
• Low heat option: Make sure "Low heat/Delicate" isn't selected by accident.
• Room: Condenser dryers struggle in very cold rooms (garages in autumn and winter), very hot rooms, or confined spaces with poor ventilation. Leave space around the vents at the front and back.

## 6. If none of that works, it's likely a fault
• Run a test: Start a timed programme and feel the drum or door after 10–15 minutes.
• No heat at all: This points to a failed heating element or a thermal cutout/thermostat. This is a common failure on these models and the parts are fairly cheap, but it involves opening the machine and mains electrics. Unplug first, or get an engineer.
• Heat but still damp: This suggests an airflow blockage still exists (check behind the condenser housing) or a fan/motor issue.
• It stops early: Revisit the sensors, or there may be a control fault.

Quick summary: In my experience, 8 times out of 10 it's a blocked condenser or softener-clogged filter, so give those a really thorough wash first.

If you let me know whether it's getting hot inside and roughly how often you've cleaned the condenser, I can help narrow it down further.
Yes, it gets hot inside the drum. I've never cleaned the condenser, I didn't know it needed doing. I'll have a go at it now.

Since it's getting hot inside, the heater is working, so a condenser that's never been cleaned is very likely the problem. Hot, moist air can't flow through a matted condenser, so the clothes stay damp.

## Cleaning the condenser
1. Unplug the dryer and let it cool down first.
2. Put a towel on the floor. Some water will come out when you remove the condenser.
3. Open the flap at the bottom front of the machine.
4. Turn the two locking levers and slide the condenser out using its handle. Keep it level, as it may hold some water.
5. Rinse it with a shower head or hose from all sides, including the front, back, and through the edges, until the water runs clear.
• If it's packed solid with fluff, soak it in warm water in the bath for a while first to loosen it.
• Don't use a pressure washer, brushes, or anything sharp. The thin fins bend easily.
6. Wipe out the cavity it sits in, plus the rubber seals on the condenser and the flap. Fluff collects there too.
7. Let it drip dry for a few minutes, then slide it back in, lock both levers firmly, and close the flap. If it isn't sealed properly, air escapes and drying stays poor.

While you're at it, also clean the door fluff filter and wipe the moisture sensor strips in the drum.

## Afterwards
• Run a normal load on Cupboard Dry rather than Iron Dry (Iron Dry intentionally leaves clothes slightly damp, which is where my last message got cut off).
• Going forward, clean the condenser every few months (roughly every 20 cycles), and the door filter after every load.

If it's still damp after this, let me know. The next things to look at would be the sensors or the condenser fan, but there's a good chance this sorts it.

Did it all. The condenser was matted with lint at the front but rinsed clean with the shower head. The door filter had a waxy film and needed a scrub, and the sensor bars were a bit dull so I wiped them with vinegar. I also vacuumed fluff out of the slot behind the condenser. Test cycle dried in about 100 minutes and the water container was nearly full.

That's fixed. A nearly full water container is the best sign: the condenser is pulling moisture out of the air again instead of recirculating it back into the clothes. 100 minutes is normal for a full load of mixed cottons, and heavier items like towels and jeans will take a bit longer.

## Keeping it working
• Door filter: Empty it after every load, and give it a rinse every few weeks. The waxy film you found suggests fabric softener build-up, so using less softener (or skipping dryer sheets) will slow that down.
• Condenser: Rinse it every couple of months, or about every 20 cycles. Now that it's clean, it'll only take a couple of minutes each time.
• Sensor bars: Wipe them with vinegar every month or two, especially if you use softener.
• Water container: Empty it every load, as you're already doing.

If drying times creep up again in future, check the condenser first. Vacuuming out the slot behind it was a good extra step, and it's worth repeating occasionally.
